nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: 06-15-94. R. E. Braun | R. G. Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Darter goby
Scientific Name:  Ctenogobius boleosoma

nodes.title: Kingdom Animalia
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Actinopterygii
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gobiidae

Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Jordan and Gilbert 1882)
	Reference for Classification (1914)
The name Gobionellus boleosoma:  invalid - subsequent name/combination

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  None

Recreational:  None

Ecological Role:  The darter goby is the most widely distributed of the scaled gobies within its range (2357). In the Indian River Lagoon in near-inlet seagrass beds, it can be one of the most abundant resident benthic species (2355; Gilmore unpub. data).  A variety of sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 2361; 2326; 672; 1862).  Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.

Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The darter goby is found along the Atlantic coast, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean from Delaware Bay to Brazil including the Bahamas (2357; 2354; 2356; 2321)

Within Study Area:  This goby is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon with greatest abundance within 7 km of ocean inlets (887; 848, 993, Gilmore unpub. data; 2355; 2320).

Mobility and Migration:
Life Mode:  The darter goby is a small, euryhaline, selective benthic feeder associated with soft sediment habitats (2357; 2356; 2355).  This species is sexually dimorphic, and has demersal eggs and planktonic larvae (2359; 2357; 2358; 2356).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  This species can be found in a wide variety of shallow, soft bottom, estuarine habitats including seagrass flats, mangroves, freshwater tributaries and canals (2357; 887; 2356; 848; 2355; 2320).  In the Indian River Lagoon, the darter goby seems to be more abundant in seagrass beds within 7 km of ocean inlets (2355; 2320; Gilmore unpub. data).

Substrate:  These gobies are generally found over soft muddy bottoms in shallow water (2357; 2358; 2356; 2360)

Physical/chemical:  This goby has been collected from waters with salinities ranging from 0.0 to 40 ppt (885; 2356; 1814; Gilmore unpub. data) and temperatures ranging from 10 to 33 C (885; Gilmore unpub. data)

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The darter goby is gonochoristic, sexually dimorphic, oviparous and has attached demersal eggs and planktonic larvae (2359; 2357; 2358; 2356).

Mating/Spawning: In North Carolina, spawning may occur from mid-March possibly through October with a peak in July and August (2358; 2321).  Hildebrand and Cable (1938) found larvae between 2.5 and 5 mm from mid-May through early November.

Fecundity: No information

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Fertilized eggs are demersal, yellow, translucent, irregularly shaped, and approximately  0.3 mm in diameter (2359; 2358).  They have much more protoplasm than yolk and have chorionic threads for attachment (2359; 2358).  Incubation period for these eggs at an unknown laboratory temperature was less than 18 hrs (2359).

Larvae:  Newly hatched larvae are 1.2 mm in length and retain a yolk-sac (2359; 2358; 2321).  By 2.5 mm, the yolk-sac is gone and the air bladder is plainly visible.  Dark pigmentation develops over air bladder and remains through 10 mm.  Notochord flexion occurs at 5 mm and all fins except spinus dorsal are fully developed by 10 mm (2359; 2358; 2321).

Juvenile:  The size of juveniles ranges from approximately 11 to as much as 22 mm (2321).  By 13 mm, the spinus dorsal is fully developed, the pigment over the air bladder is indistinct, and some adult pigmentation has developed (2358).

Adult:  Mature gravid females have been collected as small as 18 mm (2356).  Maturity has definitely been reached by 25-30 mm (2358).  Adults may reach at least 62 mm (2356; 788).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Carle and Hastings (1982) found that the darter goby selectively sieves meiofaunal organisms from bites of sediment.  Copepods, Foraminifera, nematodes and ostracods were the main items present in the gut in decreasing order of abundance.  When compared with core samples of the sediment taken at the time of fish collection, copepods and ostracods were present in greater percentages in the gut than in the sediment.  The fish retained smaller numbers of Foraminifera relative to what was available in the sediment, while nematodes were present in approximately the same proportions in both guts and cores.  Other minor items in the gut included copepod nauplii, molluscs, polychaetes, oligochaetes and some incidentally ingested plant matter.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The darter goby is the most widely distributed of the scaled gobies within its range (2357). In the Indian River Lagoon in near-inlet seagrass beds, it can be one of the most abundant resident benthic species (2355; Gilmore unpub. data).  A variety of sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 2361; 2326; 672; 1862).  Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.

Life Mode:  The darter goby is a small, euryhaline, selective benthic feeder associated with soft sediment habitats (2357; 2356; 2355).  This species is sexually dimorphic, and has demersal eggs and planktonic larvae (2359; 2357; 2358; 2356).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  This species can be found in a wide variety of shallow, soft bottom, estuarine habitats including seagrass flats, mangroves, freshwater tributaries and canals (2357; 887; 2356; 848; 2355; 2320).  In the Indian River Lagoon, the darter goby seems to be more abundant in seagrass beds within 7 km of ocean inlets (2355; 2320; Gilmore unpub. data).

Substrate:  These gobies are generally found over soft muddy bottoms in shallow water (2357; 2358; 2356; 2360)

Physical/chemical:  This goby has been collected from waters with salinities ranging from 0.0 to 40 ppt (885; 2356; 1814; Gilmore unpub. data) and temperatures ranging from 10 to 33 C (885; Gilmore unpub. data)

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  The darter goby is gonochoristic, sexually dimorphic, oviparous and has attached demersal eggs and planktonic larvae (2359; 2357; 2358; 2356).

Mating/Spawning: In North Carolina, spawning may occur from mid-March possibly through October with a peak in July and August (2358; 2321).  Hildebrand and Cable (1938) found larvae between 2.5 and 5 mm from mid-May through early November.

Fecundity: No information

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Fertilized eggs are demersal, yellow, translucent, irregularly shaped, and approximately  0.3 mm in diameter (2359; 2358).  They have much more protoplasm than yolk and have chorionic threads for attachment (2359; 2358).  Incubation period for these eggs at an unknown laboratory temperature was less than 18 hrs (2359).

Larvae:  Newly hatched larvae are 1.2 mm in length and retain a yolk-sac (2359; 2358; 2321).  By 2.5 mm, the yolk-sac is gone and the air bladder is plainly visible.  Dark pigmentation develops over air bladder and remains through 10 mm.  Notochord flexion occurs at 5 mm and all fins except spinus dorsal are fully developed by 10 mm (2359; 2358; 2321).

Juvenile:  The size of juveniles ranges from approximately 11 to as much as 22 mm (2321).  By 13 mm, the spinus dorsal is fully developed, the pigment over the air bladder is indistinct, and some adult pigmentation has developed (2358).

Adult:  Mature gravid females have been collected as small as 18 mm (2356).  Maturity has definitely been reached by 25-30 mm (2358).  Adults may reach at least 62 mm (2356; 788).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Carle and Hastings (1982) found that the darter goby selectively sieves meiofaunal organisms from bites of sediment.  Copepods, Foraminifera, nematodes and ostracods were the main items present in the gut in decreasing order of abundance.  When compared with core samples of the sediment taken at the time of fish collection, copepods and ostracods were present in greater percentages in the gut than in the sediment.  The fish retained smaller numbers of Foraminifera relative to what was available in the sediment, while nematodes were present in approximately the same proportions in both guts and cores.  Other minor items in the gut included copepod nauplii, molluscs, polychaetes, oligochaetes and some incidentally ingested plant matter.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: The darter goby is the most widely distributed of the scaled gobies within its range (2357). In the Indian River Lagoon in near-inlet seagrass beds, it can be one of the most abundant resident benthic species (2355; Gilmore unpub. data).  A variety of sparids, sciaenids, lutjanids, flatfish and barracuda, among others, consume various gobiid species (163; 664; 702; 2361; 2326; 672; 1862).  Because of the abundance and consumption by a wide variety of predators, gobies undoubtedly play an important trophic role in most low latitude estuaries.
